I've attached NO2 (Q3 2023 average) data for 33 London boroughs and a list showing which boroughs are geographic neighbors of each other.

Question: You can use a statistical method such as Getis-Ord Gi*, or any other method you choose, to identify boroughs where there is an unusually intense CONCENTRATION of high NO2 (Q3 2023 average) (a HOT spot) or low NO2 (Q3 2023 average) (a COLD spot), considering each borough TOGETHER WITH its neighbors as one combined local area.

This is different from asking whether a borough simply resembles its immediate neighbors -- instead, you are testing whether the COMBINED total (the borough together with its neighbors) is unusually large or small compared to the citywide average, regardless of how similar the borough is to any one neighbor individually.

Note: a borough whose own value is missing should not itself be reported as a hot or cold spot in your final answer. Note: dedicated spatial-statistics packages (pysal, esda, libpysal, geopandas, or similar) are NOT installed in this environment -- don't spend turns trying different import paths for them. Implement your chosen method directly using only pandas and numpy. If your method produces a z-score, use the standard critical values: |z| > 1.96 for 95% confidence, |z| > 2.576 for 99% confidence.

End your response with exactly one line listing every borough you identified, using HOT for hot spot and COLD for cold spot, and including the computed real number (e.g. a z-score) for each:
FINAL ANSWER: BoroughName1 (HOT, z-score = <value>), BoroughName2 (COLD, z-score = <value>), ... (z-score is just an example label -- if your method produces a different statistic, use its name instead, but the value after '=' must be a real number)

If you find none, write: FINAL ANSWER: none

To do this, I will iterate through each borough, find its neighbors, and sum their NO2 values. After calculating the combined values, I will compute the mean and standard deviation for these combined areas to identify hot and cold spots using z-scores.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Load the datasets again
no2_data = pd.read_csv('chunks_csv/getisord/getisord_no2_Q3_2023.csv')
adjacency_data = pd.read_csv(ADJACENCY_PATH)

# Create a dictionary to hold combined NO2 values
combined_no2 = {}

# Iterate through each borough to calculate combined NO2 values
for borough in no2_data['borough']:
    # Get the neighbors for the borough
    neighbors = adjacency_data[adjacency_data['borough'] == borough]['neighbor'].tolist()
    # Include the borough itself in the list
    all_boroughs = [borough] + neighbors
    
    # Calculate the combined NO2 value
    combined_value = no2_data[no2_data['borough'].isin(all_boroughs)]['avg_no2_value'].sum()
    
    # Store the combined value if the borough's own value is not NaN
    if not pd.isna(no2_data[no2_data['borough'] == borough]['avg_no2_value'].values[0]):
        combined_no2[borough] = combined_value

# Convert the combined values to a DataFrame for further analysis
combined_no2_df = pd.DataFrame(list(combined_no2.items()), columns=['borough', 'combined_no2_value'])

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the combined NO2 values
mean_combined_no2 = combined_no2_df['combined_no2_value'].mean()
std_combined_no2 = combined_no2_df['combined_no2_value'].std()

mean_combined_no2, std_combined_no2

This will help me identify which boroughs are hot spots (z > 1.96) and cold spots (z < -1.96). I will create a new DataFrame to store the z-scores along with the borough names.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Load the datasets again
no2_data = pd.read_csv('chunks_csv/getisord/getisord_no2_Q3_2023.csv')
adjacency_data = pd.read_csv(ADJACENCY_PATH)

# Create a dictionary to hold combined NO2 values
combined_no2 = {}

# Iterate through each borough to calculate combined NO2 values
for borough in no2_data['borough']:
    # Get the neighbors for the borough
    neighbors = adjacency_data[adjacency_data['borough'] == borough]['neighbor'].tolist()
    # Include the borough itself in the list
    all_boroughs = [borough] + neighbors
    
    # Calculate the combined NO2 value
    combined_value = no2_data[no2_data['borough'].isin(all_boroughs)]['avg_no2_value'].sum()
    
    # Store the combined value if the borough's own value is not NaN
    if not pd.isna(no2_data[no2_data['borough'] == borough]['avg_no2_value'].values[0]):
        combined_no2[borough] = combined_value

# Convert the combined values to a DataFrame for further analysis
combined_no2_df = pd.DataFrame(list(combined_no2.items()), columns=['borough', 'combined_no2_value'])

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the combined NO2 values
mean_combined_no2 = combined_no2_df['combined_no2_value'].mean()
std_combined_no2 = combined_no2_df['combined_no2_value'].std()

# Calculate z-scores for each borough
combined_no2_df['z_score'] = (combined_no2_df['combined_no2_value'] - mean_combined_no2) / std_combined_no2

# Identify hot and cold spots
hot_spots = combined_no2_df[combined_no2_df['z_score'] > 1.96]
cold_spots = combined_no2_df[combined_no2_df['z_score'] < -1.96]

hot_spots_list = hot_spots[['borough', 'z_score']]
cold_spots_list = cold_spots[['borough', 'z_score']]

hot_spots_list, cold_spots_list
```
